info.title: Nexla Rest API
info.description:
# Introduction

The Nexla API is a REST-ful API used to easily create and manage resources in Nexla in ways that best fit any use case. It can be used to configure and monitor data flows for different data-integration use cases and to perform all aspects of data engineering automation offered by the Nexla platform.

The Nexla API supports all data flow-creation and -management actions in the platform, as well as administrative user- and organization-level account-management tasks. Note that all other client packages, such as the Nexla CLI and Nexla UI, also connect to the overall Nexla infrastructure through the Nexla API.

The API references in this document lists all API endpoints and the corresponding payloads.

Check out the [API Developer Guides](https://developers.nexla.com/docs/nexla-api) to view guides and tutorials for recommended use cases for different endpoints.

# API Data Format and Versions

The API uses JSON for all data exchanges.

You __should__ specify the API version that should be used in the Accept header of each request. For example, to access Version 1 of the API, the Accept header should be the following:
```
Accept: application/vnd.nexla.api.v1+json
```

The Nexla API also supports a generic version header, which will default your access to the latest version of the data source/destination API.


```
Accept: application/json
```

# Authentication

Most Nexla API endpoints require `Bearer Token` authentication mechanism for making an authenticated request to the API. While this token can be generated programmatically outside Nexla UI by starting a session with an `api_key`, unless unavoidable, we recommend starting your session from the Nexla UI and using the `Nexla Session Token` from the Nexla UI as the Authorization header for calls to the Nexla API.

tags.name: Code Containers
tags.description:
Code containers are a general-purpose resource in the platform for storing user-defined functions that can be referenced by different modules for different purposes.

These containers can either hold the code in the database or reference the repository where the code is saved.

Common use cases are - 
1. `transform` for code blocks that are used to transform Nexsets.
2. `ai_function` for code blocks that can be used for AI functions.

For convenience, in addition to allowing direct access to any type of code_container, the API also provides some aliased versions of commonly used types of code containers. For ex, all endpoints for `transforms` are just aliases to endpoints for code_containers that can only be used for transforming Nexset record,

post.description:
Use this endpoint to preview the structure/hierarchy of storage to which this credential grants access. For example, you can use this endpoint to see the folder and file structure of a file storage system or the table-column structure of a database.
This can be used to inspect the directory hierarchy of file content storage or the database schema of a database/warehouse storage system. Note that this endpoint is only valid for credentials for storage systems wherein a storage structure needs to be reviewed.

parameters.name: credential_id
parameters.description: The unique ID of the credential being used.

parameters.name: async
parameters.description: If set to 'true', request will be executed in a deferred way, and results will be provided later.

parameters.name: request_id
parameters.description: The unique ID of the asynchronous request. In case it's provided, returns info about the deferred request.

depth.description:
Specify the hierarchy depth that should be scanned and returned in the response. 

If no other payload properties are provided, the depth is relative to the storage root. If this request contains instructions about the slice of storage to be previewed (using the path/database/table properties), the depth will be applied relative to that storage slice.

We recommend using a depth = 1 to ensure that only small, relevant slices of the storage system are scanned.

path.description:
Folder or subfolder path for which you wish to retrieve the content structure. The path string should be structured from the root of the location to the credential. For example, `demo-out.nexla.com/users/test` will return the folder tree for the contents of the `test` subfolder.

This is relevant for file-type connectors.

depth.description:
Specify the hierarchy depth that should be scanned and returned in the response. 

If no other payload properties are provided, the depth is relative to the storage root. If this request contains instructions about the slice of storage to be previewed (using the path/database/table properties), the depth will be applied relative to that storage slice.

We recommend using a depth = 1 to ensure that only small, relevant slices of storage are scanned.

database.description:
Name of the database from which you wish to fetch table names or collections. 

Relevant for Database and NoSql document-type connectors.

table.description:
Name of the table of which you wish to fetch the column structure. 

Relevant for database-type connectors.

post.description:
Use this endpoint to preview the data content in a storage system.

1. For file systems, this can be used to preview the file content of any specific file. 
2. For database systems, it can be used to preview sample rows from a table or query result. 
3. For the rest connector, it can be used to preview the results of any API request.
4. For streaming connectors, it can be used to preview some records in a topic.

For most connectors, it can also be used to determine the type of records that might be detected in the resulting Nexset.

put.description:
Update a flow's mutable fields.

Matches Rails flows_controller.rb update action and FlowNode.flow_update_mutable!():
- name: Updates flow name (propagates to resource if flow_name supported)
- description: Updates flow description (propagates to resource)
- project_id: Changes flow's project assignment (requires manage permission)
- flow_type: Changes flow type (validates replication flow constraints)
- owner_id: Changes flow owner (triggers flow_chown!)

Returns the updated flow tree via render_flows().

- project_id: Changes flow's project assignment (requires manage permission)
- flow_type: Changes flow type (validates replication flow constraints)
- owner_id: Changes flow owner (triggers flow_chown!)

Returns the updated flow tree via render_flows().

put.description:
To activate the entire flow, use either the `origin_node_id` from any data source, set or sink in the flow, or include the ?all=1 or ?full_tree=1 query parameter.
  
>**Note**: 
> 1. All endpoints for activating or pausing a flow operate on the specific resource given and all of the flow nodes downstream from that resource. This allows for pausing and activating sub-flows while leaving the rest of the flow state unchanged.
> 
>  2. You can also activate a flow by using the id of the `data_source`/ `data_set` / `data_sink` that the flow node is linked to. See relevant endpoints in the API references for those resources.

parameters.name: flow_id
parameters.description: The unique ID of the flow that needs to be activated.

parameters.name: all
parameters.description:
Set this query parameter if the flow node ID you are making a call with is not an origin flow node but you want to activate the full flow chain.
Not necessary if the flow node is an origin flow node.

put.description:

post.description:
Creates a Nexset from another Nexset.

The endpoint accepts a parent Nexset ID along with all transform and validation rules that should be applied to the parent Nexset. 

The two payload variants reflect the following two ways of specifying transform rules: 
1. Attach the transform code that should be applied: Set `has_custom_transform: false`, and attach a `transform` code snippet. 
2. Use the ID of a reusable record transform: Set `has_custom_transform: false`, and attach the `transform_id` of the record transform to be applied.

get.description: Retrieves all lookups (data maps) accessible to the authenticated user.

post.description:
Creates a new static data map in the authenticated user's account. Dynamic data maps can only be created by creating a Destination (Sink) of the type `data_map`. 

For statically assigned data maps, you can choose to add data rows to the data map by either of the following methods:
1. Send data map entries with this request. In this case, the rows of data are sent as a `data_map` array of objects.
2. Send data map entries as a separate call to add/update entries. 

You must include `map_primary_key` to specify which map attribute should be used for data matching.

get.description:
Retrieves a data map object if a valid ID is provided.

This call to `/data_maps` **does not** return data map entries, as they can be a large array of objects for big data maps. 

You can include the `expand` query parameter to fetch the data map entries of smaller static data maps.

parameters.name: data_map_id
parameters.description: The unique ID of the data map that needs to be fetched.

put.description:
Updates a data map in the authenticated user's account.

This endpoint is suitable for updating the metadata of a data map. We recommend using the data map entries update and delete endpoints to update data map rows.

parameters.name: data_map_id
parameters.description: The unique ID of the data map that needs to be updated.

delete.description: Deletes a data map from your Nexla account.

parameters.name: data_map_id
parameters.description: The unique ID of the data map that needs to be deleted.

patch.description:
Update an existing data map.

Matches Rails PUT /data_maps/{id} endpoint.

Request body (all fields optional):

post.description:
Use this endpoint for authentication if your organization allows basic authentication. A successful authentication attempt will result in an `access_token` that can be used to make authenticated requests to other API endpoints. The `access_token` automatically expires after a fixed duration, but you can also call the `/logout` endpoint to invalidate the access token at the end of your session.

Nexla supports various methods of authentication, including Basic (email/password), Google SSO, and custom SAML- or OIDC-based SSO. One or more of these methods might be allowed in any organization, depending on the configuration chosen by the administrators. Instead of using this endpoint to start a session programmatically, we recommend performing authentication through the Nexla UI and using the Nexla Session Token (available in Tools >> Nexla Session Token) to connect to the API programmatically.

> Note: A user might belong to multiple organizations. This method initiates an authenticated session in their default organization.

put.description:
Generate access token.

Replicates Rails: TokenController#create

Supports multiple authentication methods via Basic auth:
- API key: Single string API key
- Service key: Single string service key
- Email/password: Base64 encoded email:password[:org_id]

Also supports Bearer token for impersonation.

Request Headers:
    Authorization: Basic <api_key>
    Authorization: Basic <base64(email:password)>
    Authorization: Basic <base64(email:password:org_id)>
    Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

Query Parameters (for impersonation):
    user_id: User ID to impersonate
    email: Email of user to impersonate
    org_id: Org context for impersonation

Returns:
    TokenResponseSchema: Access token with user and org info

post.description: Ends the current session and invalidates the `NexlaSessionToken` for future requests.

put.description:
Invalidate access token (logout).

Replicates Rails: TokenController#invalidate

Adds the token to Redis invalidation cache, preventing future use.

Request Headers:
    Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

Returns:
    200 OK on success

get.description:
Debug endpoint showing base URL, request info and the process environment.

Rails (api_auth_configs_controller.rb:27-39)::

    def info
      head :not_found and return if !current_user.super_user?
      re = Hash.new
      request.env.each do |k, v|
        re[k] = v if v.is_a?(String)
      end
      render json: {
        :base_url => ApiAuthConfig.generate_base_url(request),
        :request_ip => request.remote_ip,
        :reqest_env => re,
        :env => ENV
      }
    end

``ENV`` extends ``Enumerable``, so ActiveSupport serializes it through
``Enumerable#as_json`` -> ``to_a.as_json`` -- an **array of ``[key, value]``
pairs**, not an object. That is the bulk of the response, and the port had
been sending ``"env": {}``.

This deliberately exposes the full process environment, secrets included
(DB password, ACCESS_TOKEN_SECRET_KEY, CREDENTIALS_ENC_KEY,
AUTH_CONFIG_ENC_KEY), because that is what the Rails endpoint does and this
port follows Rails.

Three things stand between that payload and a caller, because the action
body above is not the whole story — the controller also carries::

    before_action :validate_api_user,
                  except: [:index_client_config, :index_sign_on_options]

    def validate_api_user
      raise Api::V1::ApiError.new(:method_not_allowed) if current_org.nil?
      authorize! :manage, current_org
    end

``info`` is not in that ``except`` list, so those two run *before* the
``head :not_found`` — the same pair the five CRUD actions in ``_crud.py``
get. They are therefore checked here first, in that order; putting them
after the super-user check would collapse all three answers back into 404.

The no-org case reached 404 rather than 405 before those guards existed:
``populate_super_user_flags`` returns without setting
``_super_user_override`` when ``org_id`` is None, so ``is_super_user_async``
fell through to its own ``if not org_id: return False``. That failed closed
— the secrets below were never reachable without an org — but 404 is not the
status Rails answers with, and the org-admin case was 404 where Rails says
403.

get.description:
List clusters — matches Rails GET /clusters.

Rails gates this on **org admin**, not super user
(clusters_controller.rb:5-7)::

    raise Api::V1::ApiError.new(:forbidden) if !current_org&.has_admin_access?(current_user)

and then scopes rather than forbids (:10)::

    scope = current_user.super_user? ? Cluster : Cluster.where(org_id: current_org&.id)

So an org admin sees their own org's clusters; only a super user sees every
org's. Requiring super_user here meant an admin could create a cluster
(create was already on the org-admin gate) and then get a 403 listing it.

get.description:
Get a cluster by ID or UID — matches Rails GET /clusters/:id.

Two gates, both from Rails, and neither is super-user-only:

* the controller-wide ``before_action`` (clusters_controller.rb:5-7) —
  org admin of the acting org;
* the action's own check (:21-23)::

      unless current_user.super_user?
        raise Api::V1::ApiError.new(:forbidden) if (@cluster.org_id != current_org&.id)
      end

So an org admin may read a cluster in their own org, and only a super user
may read another org's. The 404-before-403 order matters: Rails resolves the
cluster first (``find_cluster_by_id_or_uid``) and only then compares orgs, so
a missing id is 404 for everyone rather than leaking existence through a 403.

delete.summary: Remove code containers from Custom Data Flow
delete.description:
Rails mode: :remove — removes only the ids given in the body.

An empty body is a **no-op**, matching Rails' actual behavior and the
data_credentials twin of this endpoint. The Rails comment at
custom_data_flows_controller.rb:76-77 says "DELETE with no input means delete
all", but the code does not do that: it builds
``input = { code_containers: [] }`` from the *pluralized model name*
(line 78-79), while both update_associations and remove_associations look up
``code_container_ids`` (custom_data_flow.rb:152, 186). The keys never match,
so ``input[input_key].blank?`` is true and both return early without
touching a row.

Not replicating the comment's intent on purpose: making an empty DELETE wipe
every association would be destructive and would diverge from both Rails'
real behavior and the existing data_credentials endpoint.

get.description:
Rails routes.rb:233 -> DataCredentialsController#iceberg_migration_status.

The s3 guard is ``raise ApiError.new(:method_not_allowed)`` with no message
(data_credentials_controller.rb:205), so a non-s3 credential answers a 405
with an EMPTY body -- returned as a bare Response, since main.py's
empty-body set is {401, 403, 404} and its Starlette handler rewrites routing
405s to 404.

Probe/authenticate data credentials.

Rails serves this action on BOTH `GET probe` and `GET probe/authenticate`
(config/routes.rb:205-206 → data_credentials#probe_authenticate). There is
no POST route — POST 404s on Rails — so this is GET-only on Python too.

With ``?async=1`` Rails calls ``process_async_request`` FIRST — before loading
or authorizing the credential — enqueuing a ``CallProbe`` task and returning
async task metadata (``request_id``) instead of probing inline. We mirror that
ordering here. Otherwise returns 200 OK on success, error details on failure.

get.description:
Get probe summary for data credentials.

Rails routes this to ``data_credential/probe#summary``
(config/routes.rb:208), i.e. the *base* ``Api::V1::ProbeController``, not
``DataCredentialsController#probe_authenticate`` which serves the sibling
``probe``/``probe/authenticate`` paths. The base action is two lines::

    def summary
      result = probe_service.authenticate
      render :json => result, :status => result[:status]
    end

(admin-api/app/controllers/api/v1/probe_controller.rb:20-23.)

So the body is the service result verbatim -- ``output`` included -- with no
``connection_type`` added and no ``verified_status`` write, which is why
this calls ``probe_summary`` rather than ``probe_authenticate``. Routing it
through the latter collapsed every success to a flat
``{"status": 200, "message": "Ok"}`` (that shape exists only to tell the
``probe_authenticate`` route to send Rails' ``head :ok``) and cut a
PaperTrail version on a read.

BREAKING for existing callers: the port-only ``limit`` query param is gone
(Rails has no such param — REQUEST_FILTERS defines no ``:limit`` key, so
Rails ignores it). FastAPI silently drops unknown query params, so a caller
still sending ``?limit=50`` gets no 422 telling them it moved — they get the
whole set. On a data source with thousands of detected nexsets that is a
large, silent change in response size. The endpoint is
infrastructure/super-user only, so the blast radius is internal tooling.

Pagination is available instead: ``?page=1&per_page=50`` reproduces the old
bounded behaviour, and Rails' own semantics apply — neither param means the
whole set, ``per_page=0`` likewise.

Known stricter-than-Rails edge, pre-existing and shared with other listings:
``?page=abc`` and ``?page=-1`` are rejected with 422 by the ``ge=0``
constraint, where Rails ``params[:page].to_i`` turns both into 0 and serves
unpaginated (api_controller.rb:158-160).

data_sets_controller.rb:294-306 searches *within* the shared-with-user scope

    scope = DataSet.shared_with_user(current_user, current_org)
    orgs  = Org.where(id: scope.pluck('distinct org_id'))
    ids   = orgs.flat_map { |org| BasicSearchExecutor.new(user, org, DataSet,
                                    params[:filters], scope).ids }.uniq
    @data_sets = scope.where(id: ids).page(@page).per_page(@per_page)

executor scopes visibility per org, so running it once with a single org
would drop rows Rails returns. Rendered through the same shared serializer
as GET /data_sets/available, which sets Rails' @shared = true.

List the data source's buckets.

Rails routes this path to a single fixed action::

    get 'probe' => 'data_sources/probe#list_buckets'

(admin-api/config/routes.rb:534 -- the sink equivalent at routes.rb:465
does the same, and :func:`probe_data_sink` already matches it.) There is no
action parameter in Rails: the sibling actions have their own paths
(probe/summary, probe/authenticate, probe/tree, ...), all of which exist
below.

This used to take an ``action`` query parameter defaulting to
"authenticate", so the bare path ran a different probe than Rails --
authenticate against the credential instead of listBuckets against the
connector. The parameter was also unusable: the request validator rejects
unknown query keys, so ``?action=`` came back as
``"The property '#/' contains additional properties ["action"] outside
of the schema when none are allowed"`` and no caller could reach the other
branches through it anyway.

Probe the source's credentials against the dataplane.

Rails ``ProbeController#test_authenticate`` (probe_controller.rb:5-17) and
``#summary`` (:19-22) render **identically** -- both are::

    result = probe_service.authenticate
    render :json => result, :status => result[:status]

so this returns the probe service's own result, with its own status, exactly
as ``/probe/summary`` below already does.

It used to call ``DataSourcesModule.test_authentication``, which returned a
fabricated ``{authenticated, message, timestamp}`` shape that Rails never
sends -- and always reported failure: ``authenticated`` was initialised to
``False`` and only reassigned inside ``if hasattr(ds, "test_authentication_")``,
a method that is defined nowhere in the model layer. So the endpoint could
not report success for any data source, with any credentials, ever, while
its sibling one route down did the real call.

Rails' async mode (``process_async_request("CallProbe", ...)``) is not
ported here; this path is the synchronous branch Rails falls through to.

Rails routes.rb:772 -> flow_nodes#flows_minimal (flow_nodes_controller.rb:57-107).

Returns the flow graph's wiring and nothing else -- just the id columns that
connect sources, sets and sinks -- for every origin flow node the caller can
page through. Infrastructure callers use it to rebuild the topology cheaply.

Three details separate it from ``/flows/all/condensed``:

* pagination is **always on**, at a default per_page of 100 (``@paginate =
  true`` unconditionally), where condensed only paginates when asked;
* the page is taken over *flow nodes*, then the three resource queries are
  filtered by the resulting origin_node_ids -- so per_page bounds flows, not
  rows returned;
* ``status`` is upcased only when it arrives as a string, and the dataplane
  filter applies only when no explicit ``org_id`` was given.

List recent runs for a flow that actually processed records.

Two-step:

1. Pull trigger records from Rails ``data_sources_run_ids`` (live, no
   rollup lag).
2. Filter to runs that have rows in metrics-http's
   ``flow_metrics_daily`` via ``PUT /runtime_flow_metrics`` — same
   source the flow-insights UI uses, so counts match the dashboard.

Triggers with no emitted records (polled-and-empty, pre-emission
error, aborted) are dropped. Today's runs may still be missing
because ``flow_metrics_daily`` is fed by the 01:30 UTC cron — they
show up the next day.

Pagination is applied to the trigger query before filtering, so a
page may return fewer than ``limit`` results when triggers in that
slice have no records.

Rails routes.rb:800 -> flows#update_samples (flows_controller.rb:733-745).

Bulk-sets samples for the data sets in one flow::

    flow_node = FlowNode.find(params[:flow_id])
    authorize! :manage, flow_node
    raise ApiError(:bad_request, "Flow is not api server") if
      flow_node.flow_type != FlowNode::Flow_Types[:api_server]
    input = MultiJson.load(request.raw_post)
    raise ApiError(:bad_request) unless input.is_a?(Hash)

                                params[:replace_samples].truthy?)

non-object body is a 400 with no message, so an empty body.

get.description:
Return the JSON schema for notifications.

Rails serves this from ``NotificationsController#show``
(notifications_controller.rb:68-72)::

    def show
      return if render_schema Notification
      @notification = Notification.find(params[:id])
      authorize! :read, @notification
    end

``render_schema`` short-circuits when ``params[:id] == 'schema'`` and renders
``Model.schema(:get|:post|:put)``, built by ``Api::V1::Schema`` from the
Ruby DSL in ``config/api/schemas/v1/`` -- not from the response model. This
now goes through :mod:`app.api.v1.shared.rails_schema`, a direct port of
that builder, whose output is byte-identical to Rails' for all three
variants.

What it replaced was ``model_json_schema()`` on three Pydantic classes,
which produced a structurally different document: ``$defs`` named after the
Python classes, only the definitions reachable from the model (51 against
Rails' 68 on a deterministic load), and none of the DSL's
``read_only``/``create``/``update`` semantics that decide which properties
appear in the post and put variants.

The gate is ``get_current_user``, not the infrastructure-or-super-user
dependency this route used to carry: ``show`` is covered by the controller's
plain ``authenticate``, and it is ``create`` that checks
``infrastructure_or_super_user?`` (line 75). Any authenticated caller can
read the schema on Rails.

get.description:
Handle the OAuth provider callback.

- On provider error: render error HTML (and postMessage to opener if origin known).
- On success: exchange code, then either auto-create credential (Mode A) or
  deliver tokens via postMessage (Mode B). OAuth1 providers send no code; their
  oauth_token/oauth_verifier reach the flow service in ``callback_params``.

Look up the stored OAuth context for *sid* and 302 to the provider.

The authorize URL is computed server-side from encrypted Redis context —
nothing the client passes (other than the opaque session id) determines
the redirect target. This closes the open-redirect surface a query-param
authorize_url would expose.

returns the popup URL + sid. The client opens the popup URL; the popup
in turn calls GET /oauth/redirect?sid=... which builds the provider
authorize URL server-side and 302-redirects to the provider.

put.description:
Activate a user account.

Matches Rails ``UsersController#activate`` with ``activate: true``
(routes.rb:150, users_controller.rb:209)::

    head :forbidden if input[:org_id].blank? && !current_user.super_user?
    if input[:org_id].blank?
      head :forbidden unless current_user.super_user?
    else
      org = Org.find_by_id(input[:org_id])
      head :not_found  if org.nil?
      head :forbidden  unless org.has_admin_access?(current_user)
    end
    @user = User.find_by_id(params[:user_id])
    head :not_found if @user.nil?
    if !org.nil?
      om = OrgMembership.where(user: @user, org: org).first
      head :bad_request if om.nil?
    end
    @user.activate!(org)
    render "show"

The org context drives the whole action: with no ``org_id`` this is a
super-user-only global activation, and with one the caller must be an admin
of THAT org and the target must already be a member of it. Activation then
flips the OrgMembership back to ACTIVE as well — without that a user reads as
ACTIVE but still fails the membership check in validate_account.

Rails also does not forbid activating yourself here, so no self-check.

put.description:
Deactivate a user account.

Rails serves this on the same ``UsersController#activate`` action with
``activate: false`` (routes.rb:151, users_controller.rb:209). After the
shared preamble in :func:`_resolve_activate_scope`::

    return if process_async_request("DeactivateUser", user_id: @user.id)
    @user.deactivate!(org, input[:pause_data_flows])
    render "show"

``deactivate!`` (user.rb:540) behaves very differently depending on the org:

* no ``org_id`` — global. Every non-deactivated org the user OWNS must be
  single-member, else 405; then those orgs and the user go DEACTIVATED.
* with ``org_id`` — scoped. The org cascades only if the user owns it (405
  when it has >1 member and is not already deactivated), the membership goes
  DEACTIVATED, and the user's own status is deliberately left untouched.

``pause_data_flows`` comes from the BODY (not the query string) and pauses
the user's owner-access origin nodes on either path.

get.description:
Get resources that can be transferred from a user.

Rails (users_controller.rb:298-311)::

    user = User.find(params[:user_id])
    authorize! :read, user
    if params.key?(:org_id)
      org = params[:org_id].blank? ? nil : Org.find(params[:org_id])
    else
      org = user.default_org
    end
    if org.present? && !user.org_member?(org)
      head :forbidden
    else
      render :json => user.transferable(org)
    end

Two things this turns on that a plain ``Query(None)`` cannot express:

* ``params.key?(:org_id)`` distinguishes an **absent** parameter from a
  **blank** one. Absent means "use the user's default org"; blank
  (``?org_id=``) means an explicit null org, which
  ``TransferUserResources.transferable`` translates to ``org_id IS NULL``.
  Both arrive as ``None`` through FastAPI, so presence is read off the raw
  query string.
* the gate is ``org_member?`` on the **target** user, and a non-member is
  ``head :forbidden`` -- an empty body.

schema.title: Response Get Transferable Resources Api V1 Users  User Id  Transferable Get

parameters.name: include_headers
parameters.description:
Set this to `true` if you wish to send any custom headers to be included in the ingested records as part of the request. 

The platform will ignore standard headers like `Authorization` and `Content-Type`. Any custom headers will be added as a `header_<header_name>` attribute in the record.

Example: The request header `NEX-HEADER: test` will be ingested as the attribute `header_NEX-HEADER` with the value `test`.

Default value: `false`

parameters.name: include_url_params
parameters.description:
Set this to `true` if you wish to send any custom query parameters to be included in the ingested records as part of the request. 

The platform will ignore standard query parameters like `api_key`. Any custom query parameters will be added as a `url_param_<param_name>` attribute in the record.

Example: The request query parameter `abc=def` will be ingested as the attribute `url_param_abc` with the value `def`.

Default value: `false`

parameters.name: force_schema_detection
parameters.description:
Usually, the platform performs Nexset schema detection only for the first few records from a new webhook. This is to avoid any unnecessary latencies in webhook record processing. 

Set this to `true` if you wish to enforce any webhook event to trigger schema detection. 

Default value: `false`

NexlaSessionToken.description:
The first step in calling the Nexla API or Nexla CLI is to fetch a Session access token by logging on to your Nexla UI instance. This ensures that your authentication is performed through your organization's preferred Identity Provider.

To fetch an access token from the Nexla UI, simply go to your Nexla UI instance, and try the route `/token`. For example, if your Nexla UI instance is at `https://dataops.nexla.io`, open `https://dataops.nexla.io/token` in the browser. 

This will automatically route you to a login page, ask you to authenticate using your preferred Identity Provider, and, upon successful authentication, route you to a page where you can copy the Access Token.

Usage format: `Bearer <JWT>`.

schema.description:
Add this query parameter to a request to view resources for which the authenticated user has permission. 

1. `collaborator`: Resources to which the user has access via the collaborator or higher permissions.
2. `operator`: Resources to which the user has access via the operator or higher permissions.
3. `admin`: Resources to which the user has access via the administrator or owner permissions.
4. `owner`: Resources created by the user.
Note that the absence of this property in the request is treated as `owner`, so you do not need to set `access_role=owner` in the query.

AccessRoles.description:
This property reflects all the permissions the user/team/organization has to this resource. 

1. `collaborator`: The user/team/organization can view the resource but not make any modifications to it.
2. `operator`: The user/team/organization can view the resource and can activate/pause it, but not make any other modifications to it.
3. `administrator`: The user/team/organization has complete administrative rights to this resource.
4. `owner`: This user created the resource and so has complete administrative rights to it.

has_ssh_tunnel.description:

Default value: `false`

__SSH Tunnel Host__: To connect via an SSH tunnel, you need to use a bastion host running an SSH tunnel server with access to your database. Enter the SSH tunnel hostname or IP address of the bastion host.

__Required__ if `has_ssh_tunnel` is `true`

__Required__ if `has_ssh_tunnel` is `true`

Default Value: `22`

tunnel.bastion.user.description:

__Required__ if `has_ssh_tunnel` is `true`

encrypt.private.password.description:
__Your Password for Private Key__: Set this to the password of the user ID used to generate the PGP private key.

__Required__ if `file_encryption_enabled` is `true` and `encrypt.standard` is `pgp`

encrypt.private.key.description:
__Your Private Key__: Enter your PGP private key. This private key (and the associated user id and password) will be used for encrypting/decrypting files.
 
__Required__ if `file_encryption_enabled` is `true` and `encrypt.standard` is `pgp`

storage.account.name.description:
__Azure Storage Account Name__: The name of the storage account that you wish to access.

__Applicable and required__ if `azure_blb.auth.type` is `SAS Token` or `Storage Account Key`

azure_blb.auth.type.description:
__Authentication Mechanism__: Credentials can be configured to allow Azure access through different authentication mechanisms. Select the type of Authentication method you wish to use.

* `SAS Token` for Shared Access Signature Token authentication.

* `Connection String` for Key Connection String authentication.

* `Storage Account Key` for Storage Account Key authentication.

sas.token.description:
__Shared Access Signature Token__: Enter the shared access signature token for the Azure storage that you wish to access.

__Required__ if `azure_blb.auth.type` is `SAS Token`

key.connection.string.description:
__Key Connection String__: Enter the Azure connection string for the Azure storage that you wish to access.

__Required__ if `azure_blb.auth.type` is `Connection String`

storage.account.key.description:
__Storage Account Key__: Enter the Azure storage account key for the Azure storage that you wish to access.

__Required__ if `azure_blb.auth.type` is `Storage Account Key`

storage.account.name.description: __Azure Storage Account Name__: The name of the storage account that you wish to access.

azure_dl.auth.type.description:
__Authentication Mechanism__: Credentials can be configured to allow Azure access through different authentication mechanisms. Select the type of Authentication method you wish to use.

* `SAS Token` for Shared Access Signature Token authentication.

* `Connection String` for Key Connection String authentication.

* `Storage Account Key` for Storage Account Key authentication.

sas.token.description:
__Shared Access Signature Token__: Enter the shared access signature token for the Azure storage that you wish to access.

__Required__ if `azure_dl.auth.type` is `SAS Token`

key.connection.string.description:
__Key Connection String__: Enter the Azure connection string for the Azure storage that you wish to access.

__Required__ if `azure_dl.auth.type` is `Connection String`

storage.account.key.description:
__Storage Account Key__: Enter the Azure storage account key for the Azure storage that you wish to access.

__Required__ if `azure_dl.auth.type` is `Storage Account Key`

host.description: __Host__: Enter the hostname for your database. This is usually an IP address or text in the format __company.domain.com__. Do not include the connection protocol.

port.description: __Port__: Enter the port used to access your database.

username.description: __Username__: Enter the username used to access your database.

password.description: __Password__: Enter the password used to access your database.

database_name.description: __Database Name__: Enter the database name if you want to connect to a specific database.

schema_name.description: __Schema Name__: Enter the schema name for the database to which you wish to connect.

database.field.applicationIntent.description:
__Connection Mode / Application Intent__: You can restrict database connectivity capabilities by specifying the connection mode. Select __Read Only__ to connect to the database in __readonly__ mode.

* `readonly`: Connect in read-only mode.

* `readwrite`: Connect in read-write mode.

Default value: `readwrite`

is_service_account.description:
__Is Service Account Authentication?__ We support multiple ways of authenticating your BigQuery account. We recommend using the Google Service Account (System User Authentication) method, as it is best suited for accessing your data and is tied to the service account instead of the individual user account.
* Set to `true` if you wish to choose Google Service Account (System User Authentication). 
* Set this to `false` if you wish to authenticate using 3-legged OAuth. 
Default Value: `false`

project_id.description: __Project ID__: The Project ID to which the database you wish to access belongs.

json_creds.description:
__Service Account JSON credentials content__: This is the content of the service account credentials JSON file generated by Google Cloud IAM, which is added to the payload as a JSON object.

__Required__ if `is_service_account` is `true`

auth.type.description:
__End User Authentication Type__: This must be set to `OAUTH2` if you are choosing the 3-legged OAuth authentication mechanism.

__Required__ if `is_service_account` is `false`

oauth2.client.id.description:
__Client ID__: The Client ID of your OAuth 2.0 client.

__Required__ if `is_service_account` is `false`

oauth2.client.secret.description:
__Client Secret__: The Client Secret of your OAuth 2.0 client.

__Required__ if `is_service_account` is `false`

oauth2.access.token.url.description:
__Access Token URL__: The OAuth 2.0 Token URL used for fetching the token from the API token server. This must be `https://www.googleapis.com/oauth2/v4/token`.

__Required__ if `is_service_account` is `false`

oauth2.token.type.override.description:
__Token Type__: The token type that should be used when attaching the OAuth2.0 token to the request. This must be `Bearer`.

__Required__ if `is_service_account` is `false`

oauth2.access.token.method.description:
__Access Token URL method__: The request method used for the OAuth 2.0 Token URL. This must be `POST`.

__Required__ if `is_service_account` is `false`

vendor.name.description:
__Nexla OAuth 2.0 connector codename__: Unique codename for the Nexla token refresh mechanism, which is used to identify this connector. This must be `bigquery`.

__Required__ if `is_service_account` is `false`

vendor.token_type.description:
__Token Type__: The token type that should be used when attaching the OAuth2.0 token to the request. This must be `Bearer`.

__Required__ if `is_service_account` is `false`

vendor.auth_scheme.description:
__Authentication Payload Mode__: Set how the OAuth 2.0 Client ID and Client Secret should be sent with the Token URL. This must be set to `header`.

__Required__ if `is_service_account` is `false`

vendor.scopes.description:
__API Scopes__: Scopes that should be added to the OAuth token calls. This should be `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/bigquery https://www.googleapis.com/auth/devstorage.read_write`.

__Required__ if `is_service_account` is `false`

vendor.refresh_url.description:
__Refresh Token URL__: The OAuth 2.0 Token Refresh URL that is used for fetching a new access token using the current access token and refresh token. This must be `https://www.googleapis.com/oauth2/v4/token`.

__Required__ if `is_service_account` is `false`

vendor.has_token_expiration_ts.description:
__Requires Auto-Refresh of Token__: Access tokens are short-lived, and the platform should automatically continuously refresh the token to retain a valid access token. This must be `true`.

__Required__ if `is_service_account` is `false`

vendor.token_expires_in.description:
__Access token expiration time__: Set this to the expiration time (in seconds) of the access token received when you made the first token request as part of the 3-legged OAuth 2.0 token fetching sequence. This is usually `3599` for a 3-legged OAuth workflow.

__Required__ if `is_service_account` is `false`

access_token.description:
__Access Token__: Set this to the access token received when you made the first token request as part of the the 3-legged OAuth 2.0 token fetching sequence.

__Required__ if `is_service_account` is `false`

vendor.access_token.description:
__Access Token__: Set this to the access token received when you made the first token request as part of the the 3-legged OAuth 2.0 token fetching sequence. Note that this is the same as `access_token` above but is required in the payload to allow Nexla to automatically continuously refresh tokens.

__Required__ if `is_service_account` is `false`

vendor.refresh_token.description:
__Refresh Token__: Set this to the refresh token received when you made the first token request as part of the the 3-legged OAuth 2.0 token fetching sequence.

__Required__ if `is_service_account` is `false`

gcs.location.description:
__GCS Location for staging data__: Before loading data from/to Bigquery, we might need to stage the data in a temporary GCS location. This temporary location is created by the platform automatically if the user has permission to create a bucket/path.

But you can override bucket creation and instead name a specific GCS location where temporary staging files will be created.

temp.table.dataset.description:
__Temporary Dataset__: Before loading data from/to BigQuery we might need to stage the data in a temporary dataset. This temporary dataset is created by the platform automatically if the user has permission to create a dataset.

However, you can override dataset creation and instead name a specific existing dataset as the temporary dataset to be used.

__Connection Mode / Application Intent__: You can restrict database connectivity capabilities by specifying the connection mode. Select __Read Only__ to connect to the database in __readonly__ mode.

* `readonly`: Connect in read-only mode.

* `readwrite`: Connect in read-write mode.

Default value: `readwrite`

has_ssh_tunnel.description:
__Requires SSH Tunnel for access?__: If your server is not publicly accessible, Nexla enables connecting via an SSH tunnel. When using this method, Nexla will connect to a bastion host via SSH, and the server connection will occur from the SSH host.

Default value: `false`

tunnel.bastion.host.description:
__SSH Tunnel Host__: To connect via an SSH tunnel, you need to use a bastion host running an SSH tunnel server with access to your database. Enter the SSH tunnel hostname or IP address of the bastion host.

__Required__ if `has_ssh_tunnel` is `true`

tunnel.bastion.port.description:
__SSH Tunnel Port__: Enter the port of the tunnel bastion host to which Nexla can connect.

__Required__ if `has_ssh_tunnel` is `true`

Default Value: `22`

tunnel.bastion.user.description:
__Username for tunnel__: As part of setting up the bastion host, you also need to create an SSH user for Nexla. Enter that username here. Usually, this is set to `nexla`.

__Required__ if `has_ssh_tunnel` is `true`

target.bootstrap.servers.description: __Kafka Bootstrap Servers__: Enter the addresses of the Kafka brokers. These are usually in the form of Virtual IP addresses.

security.protocol.description:
__Security Protocol__: Choose the appropriate security protocol for your Kafka channels.

* `SASL_SSL`: SASL-authenticated SSL channel

sasl.jaas.username.description: __Confluent Cloud API Key__: Enter the API Key for the Confluent Cloud cluster.

sasl.jaas.password.description: __Confluent Cloud API Secret__: Enter the API Secret required to connect to the Confluent Cloud cluster.

group.id.prefix.description:
__Consumer Group ID__: Enter the  Group ID of the group to which Nexla consumers will belong.

This is usually set to `nexla-consumer`.

databricks_auth_type.description:
__Authentication Type__: Select the authentication type for your databricks instance.

* `token` - Token Based Authentication: Use this authentication method if you are using a personal access token to authenticate with Databricks. See https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/auth/pat#pat-user for more information.
  
* `oidc` -  OAuth Authentication: Use this authentication method if you are using OAuth2.0 to authenticate with Databricks. This method is recommended for production environments.

ui.url_format.description:
__URL Format__: You can set the Databricks authentication information as a JDBC URL or as parts that will be combined by Nexla to create the connection string.

* `jdbc_url` - JDBC URL: Set the JDBC URL to your databricks location. This should be in the form `jdbc:spark:/...` or `jdbc:databricks:/...`.

* `http_path_parts` - HTTP Path Parts: Set the HTTP Path for the SQL Endpoint. This is usually in the form `sql/protocolv1/o/<id>/0916-102516-naves603` and available in __JDBC settings__ in your databricks console.

url.description:
__JDBC URL__: Enter the JDBC URL to your databricks location. This should be in the form `jdbc:databricks:/...` or `jdbc:spark:/...`.

**Note**: For **OAuth Authentication** please ensure that the URL does not include the `AuthMech` and `Auth_Flow` parameters. The Databricks Console for copying connection strings often includes these parameters, so you may need to remove them before using the connection string in Nexla.

__Required__ if `ui.url_format` is `jdbc_url`.

host.description:
__Host__: Enter the hostname for your database. This is in the format `company.domain.com`. Do not include the connection protocol.
__Required__ if `ui.url_format` is `http_path_parts`.

port.description:
__Port__: Enter the port used to access your database.
__Required__ if `ui.url_format` is `http_path_parts`.

http_path.description:
__HTTP Path__: Enter the HTTP Path of the SQL Endpoint.
This is usually in the form `sql/protocolv1/o/<id>/0916-102516-naves603` and is available in __JDBC settings__ in your Databricks console.
__Required__ if `ui.url_format` is `http_path_parts`.

username.description:
__Username__: Enter the username used to access your database.
__Required__ if `ui.url_format` is `http_path_parts`.

password.description:
__Password__: Enter the password used to access your database.
__Required__ if `databricks_auth_type` is `token` and `ui.url_format` is `http_path_parts`.

databricks.field.AuthMech.description:
__OAuth2 Authentication Mechanism__: Set the authentication mechanism for your databricks instance.
__Required__ if `databricks_auth_type` is `oidc`.
__Applicable__ only if `databricks_auth_type` is `oidc`.

databricks.field.Auth_Flow.description:
__OAuth2 Authentication Flow__: Set the authentication flow for your databricks instance.
__Required__ if `databricks_auth_type` is `oidc`.
__Applicable__ only if `databricks_auth_type` is `oidc`.

databricks.field.OAuth2ClientId.description:
__Service Principal UUID/Application ID__: Enter the Service Principal UUID/Application ID for the Databricks warehouse you wish to connect to.
__Required__ if `databricks_auth_type` is `oidc`.
__Applicable__ only if `databricks_auth_type` is `oidc`.

databricks.field.OAuth2Secret.description:
__Service Principal Secret__: Enter the Service Principal Secret for the Databricks you wish to connect to.
__Required__ if `databricks_auth_type` is `oidc`.
__Applicable__ only if `databricks_auth_type` is `oidc`.

database_name.description:
__Database Name__: Enter the database name if you want to connect to a specific database.
Usually, this is set to: `spark`.

schema_name.description:
__Schema Name__: Enter the schema name for the database to which you wish to connect.
Usually, this is set to `default`.

databricks.cloud.type.description:
__Databricks Cloud Type__: Select the cloud environment type of your Databricks instance.
Usually, this is the Databricks cloud environment, but we also support connecting to Databricks instances running in other cloud environments.

databricks.cloud.credentials.id.description:
__Nexla Credential ID for temporary data staging__: Before loading data to Databricks we need to stage the data temporarily. In the default configuration, the staging data is stored in a Nexla private location, but you can configure the platform to stage data in your custom Cloud storage location.
Enter the __Nexla Credential ID__ of your S3 or Azure Blob storage account where you want Nexla to write temporary and final data. Leave this blank if you want Nexla to handle temporary data storage.
__Applicable__ if `databricks.cloud.type` is `AWS` or `Azure`.
Ignore this property if you do not want to use your custom data-staging area.

databricks.temp.s3.bucket.description:
__S3 Path for Temporary Data Staging__: If you are choosing to store temporary data in your own AWS S3 location, please configure the S3 path where the temporary data should be staged. Note that this path must be accessible to the Nexla Credential ID entered in the previous field.
__Applicable and required__ only if `databricks.cloud.type` is `AWS` and you are setting a valid credential ID for `databricks.cloud.credentials.id`.

databricks.destination.s3.bucket.description:
__S3 Path for Delta Tables__: If you are choosing to store temporary data in your own AWS S3 location, please configure the S3 path where the delta tables should be staged. Note that this path must be to Nexla Credential ID provided earlier.
Leave this blank for creating Delta tables in DBFS.
__Applicable and required__ only if `databricks.cloud.type` is `AWS` and you are setting a valid credential ID for `databricks.cloud.credentials.id`.

databricks.temp.azure.bucket.description:
__Azure Path for Temporary Data Staging__: If you are choosing to store temporary data in your own Azure Blob location, please configure the path where the temporary data should be created. Note that this path must be accessible to the Nexla Credential ID entered in the previous field.
__Applicable and required__ only if `databricks.cloud.type` is `Azure` and you are setting a valid credential ID for `databricks.cloud.credentials.id`.

databricks.destination.azure.bucket.description:
__Azure Path for Delta Tables__: If you are choosing to store temporary data in your own Azure Blob location, please configure the path where the delta tables should be created. Note that this path must be accessible to the Nexla Credential ID provided earlier.
Leave this blank for creating Delta tables in DBFS.
__Applicable and required__ only if `databricks.cloud.type` is `Azure` and you are setting a valid credential ID for `databricks.cloud.credentials.id`.

s3_auth_type.description:
__Authentication Mechanism__ Credentials can be configured to allow S3 access through different AWS permissions mechanisms. Select the type of Authentication method you wish to use.
* `Access Key` - Select this option if you wish to use AWS Access and Secret keys for your S3 access.
* `ARN` - Select this option if you wish to use IAM ARN for authentication.
* `Instance Role` - Select this option if you wish to access S3 using an IAM Instance Role.

external_id.description:
__External Id__: The external ID if S3 has been configured for federated access.

__Required__ if `s3_auth_type` is `ARN`

region.description:
Region for AWS S3 Account.

Default value: `us-east-1`

arn.description: __IAM ARN__: The IAM Amazon Resource Name (ARN) for which these permissions are applicable. This should be entered in the format `arn:partition:service:region:account:resource`.

test.path.description: __S3 Path list access is limited to__: Set this property to `<bucket-name>` or `<bucket-name>/<folder-name>` if your AWS admin has restricted access to only a specific bucket or a path inside a bucket.

has_client_encryption.description:
__Enable Client Side Encryption?__: The platform can be configured to encrypt/decrypt S3 objects that require client-side encryption using the AWS Key Management System (KMS). Set this option if KMS encryption is applicable.

Default value: `false`

encryption_mode.description:
__Client Side Encryption Mode__ : Select the type of KMS encryption mode that is applicable for this credential.

__Required__ if `has_client_encryption` is `true`

kms_key.description:
__Amazon KMS Key for Encryption__: The KMS Key used for encrypting/decrypting objects. Please ensure that this user has appropriate KMS permissions.

__Required__ if `has_client_encryption` is `true`

sse.enabled.description:
__Enable Server Side Encryption?__: The platform can be configured to encrypt/decrypt S3 objects that require server-side encryption.

This can be achieved using either __Amazon S3-managed encryption keys (SSE-S3)__ or the __AWS Key Management Service (SSE-KMS)__. Set this option if server-side encryption is applicable.

Default value: `false`

sse.kms_key.arn.description:
__Key ARN for SSE with KMS__: The Key ARN if you want server-side encryption to be performed via the AWS Key Management System. You can leave this blank if you want to use Amazon S3-managed encryption keys.

__Required__ if `sse.enabled` is `true`

access_token.description: __Access Token__: Access token used to connect to your Dropbox account. See the Dropbox developer documentation for instructions on how to generate an access token.

auth_type.description:
__Authentication Mechanism__: Credentials can be configured to allow access through different AWS permissions mechanisms. Select the type of Authentication method you wish to use.

- __Access Key__: Use your AWS Access Key and Secret Key to authenticate.

dynamodb.endpoint.description:
__DynamoDB Endpoint__: Endpoint for accessing your DynamoDB instance. Usually of the form `dynamodb.us-east-2.amazonaws.com`.

__Applicable and required__ if `auth_type` is `Access Key`.

access.key.description:
__AWS Access Key__: Your AWS Access Key.

__Applicable and required__ if `auth_type` is `Access Key`.

secret.key.description:
__AWS Secret Key__: Your AWS Secret Key.

__Applicable and required__ if `auth_type` is `Access Key`.

dynamodb.region.description:
__Region__: AWS Region for DynamoDB. Defaults to `us-east-1`.

__Applicable__ if `auth_type` is `Access Key`.

is_service_account.description:
__Authentication Type__: We currently only support __System User Authentication__ method as it is best suited for accessing your own data and is tied to a service account instead of an individual user account. Please contact your Nexla support team if you need __End User Authentication__ mechanism.

* `true`: __System User Authentication__
* `false`: __End User Authentication__ (Currently not supported)

project_id.description:
__Project ID__: Enter the Project ID that the Firebase store you wish to access belongs to.

__Applicable and required__ if `is_service_account` is `false`.

json_creds.description:
__Credentials File Content__: Enter the content of the JSON file that contains the Firebase service account credentials. This file is usually downloaded from the Firebase console.

__Applicable and required__ if `is_service_account` is `true`.

port.description: __Port__: Enter the port used to access your database.

username.description: __Username__: Enter the username used to access your database.

password.description: __Password__: Enter the password used to access your database.

host.description: __Host__: Enter the FTP server URL. Do not include the connection protocol.

port.description:
